I think it's more that good people make bad politicians than anything else. There are two main problems.

  • Being a politician fundamentally comes down to making people like you or want to vote for you. But these same voters are often quick to turn against you if they find out you stand against something that's important to them. Take two voters, both of whom you need to vote for you, and they'll probably have a number of mutually exclusive beliefs. If you don't go against one's core values in some way or another, you're probably going to end up going against the other. And this is before you even get into your own personal beliefs which are further mutually exclusive. If people all know your actual positions on things, you'd probably do pretty poorly. Think of all the, "Yeah I really support Ron Paul on [this this this and that] but then there's this one issue..." There's no particularly great way to overcome this while remaining at all ethical.

  • The above point isn't even the real problem. The real problem is messaging. If you want to be a politician you need to get your message out. How do you do that? Money - lots and lots of money. Where does that money come from? Primarily big corporations looking to exploit the people, the ones that you need to like you, for the sake of profit. I think that is basically just impossible to ethically reconcile. Corporations aren't going to give you substantial amounts of money unless you're furthering their interests - and their interests are in the majority of cases directly against the interests of the people you need to vote for you. Bernie showed that it's possible to get funding through a grass roots effort, but he was still crushed by the money big business and SuperPACs were throwing at Hillary. They know she'll give them what they want and so consequently sending hundreds of millions her way is seen as little more than an investment. How do you pull in a competitive amount of money while also staying on the up and up? Again, I don't think there's really any way.

I think you guys fundamentally misdiagnose the type of person who wants to be a politician.

Politicians are skilled in getting people to like them. That is what gives a politician his power: not any intrinsic strength or intellect or ability of his own - only that people like them and are prepared to tick their box rather than the other guy's. Likeability has little to do with assessing the character of the other: as every con man knows, intellectual reasoning can be easily overridden by techniques devoted to persuasion ... or to telling the person what they want to hear, which is a technique of persuasion in itself, since we tend to like those who are in any way like us, and someone who thinks the way we do has to be like us.

What sort of person rests their whole professional life on the prospect of getting others to like them? The sort of person who gets a huge adrenalin rush out of the affirmation of being elected. That is, a person with no sense of their own intrinsic worth; a person with low self-esteem; a person who will change what they are, who they are, for the sake of shifting alliances. A person who has no concrete moral principles against either the mob that he kowtows to or the institution that he parasitises. Thus Bernie Sanders: I had no doubt he would eventually back Hilary Clinton. The Left believes in the Party, not the people, and Sanders has battened off the blood of the Democratic Party all his adult life.

The only principle a politician holds to is pragmatism. Any others are cast aside or compromised shortly after he gains office. Thus why so many politicians are corrupt or succumb: if you have cast away even your most cherished principles for the sake of power, and have found that power is usable to avoid laws to which you are otherwise bound, what incentive is there for you to obey the law past the point of what can be proven against you?

Put it this way: if you read Robert Greene's 48 Laws of Power, you'll get a taste of what politicians live and breathe every day of their lives, even if they apply the laws to a greater or lesser extent. I -- and in a decent world, I hope you -- went away from that book feeling pretty dirty. The standard Instagram attention whore is a larval, primitive form of the politician.
